story.title: Supreme Court to Review Trump's Asylum Ban Authority
story.summary: The Supreme Court will decide if the Trump administration has the authority to ban asylum claims at the southern border. This case arises from lower court rulings that deemed the executive order illegal, as federal law permits individuals to seek asylum based on fears of persecution, regardless of their entry method into the U.S.

explore_lenses.label: What did the proclamation change at the border?
explore_lenses.title: A new summary-removal framework
explore_lenses.summary: The January 20, 2025 proclamation suspended entry for people crossing the southern border outside designated ports and for undocumented arrivals at ports, while directing agencies to repatriate or remove covered people. The legal challenge concerns the accompanying procedures after a person is physically present in the United States, not the President’s authority to suspend entry itself.

claims.text: Proclamation 10888 directs the Homeland Security Secretary, in coordination with the State Department and attorney general, to repel, repatriate, or remove people covered by the entry suspension until the President finds the asserted “invasion” has ended.
The D.C. Circuit described the implementation as using new summary-removal procedures that omit the usual statutory opportunities to seek asylum and other removal protections.
The administration maintains that the restrictions are necessary to restore operational control of the border and to address claimed public-safety and national-security risks.

explore_lenses.label: What legal question will the justices confront?
explore_lenses.title: Entry power versus congressionally set procedures
explore_lenses.summary: The central dispute is whether statutes allowing a president to suspend or restrict entry also permit the executive branch to bypass the Immigration and Nationality Act’s procedures and protections for people already in the country. The lower court held that they do not.

claims.text: The administration relies principally on 8 U.S.C. §§ 1182(f) and 1185(a), arguing that they authorize suspension of entry and categorical denial of asylum applications that it regards as inevitably unsuccessful.

The D.C. Circuit held that those provisions authorize entry restrictions but do not authorize the executive branch to replace the INA’s removal procedures or bar access to asylum and withholding protections for people already present in the United States.

The appeals court also found that the policy could not displace statutory withholding-of-removal protections or required Convention Against Torture procedures, which can bar removal to a country where persecution or torture risks meet the relevant legal standards.

explore_lenses.label: What happens while the case is pending?
explore_lenses.title: The policy remains operative for now
explore_lenses.summary: Reporting on November 13 said the asylum ban had remained in effect through the litigation, while the Supreme Court agreed to consider the administration’s appeal. The Court’s public docket showed the petition had been distributed for its November 13 conference, but did not yet display a merits briefing or argument schedule in the version consulted.

claims.text: The Supreme Court docket identifies the case as Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, No. 26-239, arising from the D.C. Circuit’s April 24, 2026 decision; the petition was distributed for the Court’s November 13, 2026 conference.
Associated Press reported on November 13 that the Court agreed to hear the case and that the asylum restrictions had remained in place during the litigation.
Forecast: AP reported that the justices were expected to hear the case in the coming months and decide it by the end of June.

story_report.summary: The Supreme Court has agreed to review the Trump administration’s restrictions on asylum claims at the southern border, taking up a dispute over whether the president may suspend entry and limit access to statutory protections. The case, Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, follows lower-court rulings that found the executive action unlawful. The restrictions have remained in effect during the litigation, leaving the Court’s eventual ruling poised to determine the scope of asylum access under the policy.

sections.heading: Border Policy and Removal Procedures
sections.body: Proclamation 10888 directs the Homeland Security secretary, working with the State Department and attorney general, to repel, repatriate or remove people covered by the entry suspension until the president finds the asserted “invasion” has ended. The D.C. Circuit described the policy’s implementation as relying on new summary-removal procedures that omit the usual statutory opportunities to seek asylum and other removal protections. The administration says the restrictions are needed to restore operational control at the border and address claimed public-safety and national-security risks.

sections.heading: Presidential Authority and Statutory Protections
sections.body: The administration principally relies on federal immigration provisions, 8 U.S.C. §§ 1182(f) and 1185(a), arguing they permit suspension of entry and categorical denial of asylum applications it considers inevitably unsuccessful. The D.C. Circuit held that those provisions allow entry restrictions but do not permit the executive branch to replace Immigration and Nationality Act removal procedures or bar people already in the United States from seeking asylum and withholding protections. The appeals court also concluded the policy could not displace withholding-of-removal or Convention Against Torture procedures.

sections.heading: Supreme Court Review Schedule
sections.body: The case stems from the D.C. Circuit’s April 24, 2026 decision, and the Supreme Court petition was distributed for the justices’ Nov. 13, 2026 conference. Associated Press reported that the justices were expected to hear arguments in the coming months and decide the case by the end of June. As of Nov. 13, however, the Court’s docket did not list an argument date, merits briefing schedule or decision date.

related_stories.title: Iran Claims Attack on US Radar System in Bahrain Amid Ongoing Tensions
related_stories.summary: Iran has claimed responsibility for targeting a US radar system in Bahrain, asserting that the system was destroyed. However, the US military's Central Command has denied this, stating that it intercepted two drones launched by Iran's Revolutionary Guards. The situation remains tense, with ongoing clashes in the Strait of Hormuz.

related_stories.title: Bessent Criticizes Lutnick's Department for Nvidia Chip Export Oversight
related_stories.summary: Scott Bessent has publicly criticized Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick's department for not restricting exports of Nvidia chips to a company believed to have connections with China. This criticism comes amid growing scrutiny of Lutnick's actions and decisions related to the Nvidia scandal, which has raised national security concerns. The situation has led to questions about the involvement of senior officials from the Trump administration in the matter.
